I build a multi-purpose mcp that runs orchestrations, task management, and git versioned project knowledge base all-in-one. So it covers the whole engineering workflow end to end for me. I started to build that thing because at my work there multiple code repos around one product. If I build something downstream for my helpdesk but need me and my agents to consider whats going on in the firmware I would usually read lots of specs. And still wouldn't know the quirks. Especially with a firmware that you don't find on the internet. 
So I build something that type of knowledge accross several repos with every task, and connects the dots. In fact curation happens as part of dev cycle and is not an afterthought that some background agent has to piece together from scraps. The project turned out to be a monster that took 8 months of my side quest time. A bit too ambitious for a solo project. But the further I got the more it could do on its own.

Dot (OpenAI) is a single always-on agent with its own cloud computer, included on ChatGPT Pro from $100/mo. Chats don't count against limits, but delegated Codex/Work tasks do.

Grok Bot is a multi-bot team on one shared computer, from ~$20-30/mo, with weekly usage pools that setup and coding can burn through (as described).

Dot favors ChatGPT/Slack users and one generalist; Grok Bot favors parallel specialists and lower entry cost. Both charge for heavy compute.

FIVE WAYS AN ALWAYS-ON AGENT FAILS, AND NONE OF THEM IS A PROMPT PROBLEM

from @0xwhrrari's guide to Grok Bot, the Grok 4.6 agent with a persistent cloud computer

most people give the bot one vague request, connect every account they own and wait for magic

the five failures and what is actually broken:
1. it forgets a preference: a state problem
2. it opens the wrong tool: a routing problem
3. it sends what should have stayed a draft: a permission problem
4. it repeats the same failed action: a loop problem
5. five bots keep asking who does what: a graph problem

worth saving, his autonomy ladder:
0. observe
1. prepare: research, draft, stage
2. execute, parking every irreversible step for approval
3. run on a schedule or trigger, with a receipt
4. coordinate specialist bots

his rule for moving up a level: at least 5 clean runs first

which level is your bot on?
